title: Connection
author: Nick Hart
summary: The third post in Nick Hart's six sense making disciplines series, adapted from Richard Claydon, argues that connection creates the relational conditions under which collective sense making can happen. Hart describes how disconnection shows up subtly in schools, through silence in meetings, guarded conversations and compliance without commitment. His central claim is that leaders cannot demand trust but can, through deliberate and repeated relational acts, make it more likely. He sets out four strategies: brief 'forced fun' that signals psychological safety, celebrating humble routine work, championing colleagues through stories, and leader-first vulnerability. He argues that without connection, coherence becomes brittle and clarity becomes mere compliance, so relational work should be treated as infrastructure rather than atmosphere.
points: Hart names the quiet signs of disconnection in schools, including compliance without commitment and energy draining into private rather than shared conversations.
Short, structured moments of humour are presented not as entertainment but as a signal of psychological safety that softens status boundaries.
Recognising routine, low-visibility work is argued to protect relational trust, because unseen effort leaves people feeling instrumental rather than valued.
Leaders going first with vulnerability, by admitting uncertainty and inviting critique before defending, widens the space for honest interpretation without diminishing authority.
Without connection, he argues, coherence becomes brittle and clarity becomes compliance, which is why connection should be treated as infrastructure rather than atmosphere.
quotes: Connection is produced through deliberate relational acts, exercised repeatedly and made visible to others. In complex systems, leaders cannot demand trust, but they can create conditions in which trust becomes more likely.
Leaders practising connection sometimes introduce lightness deliberately. Short, structured moments of humour or play disrupt hierarchy and soften status boundaries.
Celebrating humble tasks signals that contribution matters at every level. When everyday effort goes unseen, relational trust erodes. People feel instrumental rather than valued.

Stories travel faster than policies. Leaders practising connection amplify examples of thoughtful practice, resilience or collaboration. They tell stories that make values concrete and contributions visible.
This does not diminish authority; it signals that sense making is shared rather than controlled. When leaders remain guarded, others follow suit. Conversation narrows, risk taking declines.
When connection is weak, coherence becomes brittle and clarity becomes compliance. People may appear aligned, but sense making becomes private and defensive.

They are not morale boosters to deploy occasionally; they are relational habits that widen participation and strengthen trust. Their phrasing is intentionally simple; they are designed to humanise systems that can otherwise become procedural.
